I had an amazing time participating in Cal Hacks 12.0 over the weekend! While there, I worked with Vaibhav Hariram and Abhinav Jinka to create Elytra – an AI-powered platform that helps businesses cut through the noise and find the right AI tools for their specific challenges. Companies are overwhelmed by the sheer number of AI solutions available, and it's difficult to know which tools actually fit their unique needs and constraints. This is where Elytra comes in. By answering a simple 5-question survey, Elytra analyzes responses and recommends the three best-fit AI tools, complete with a compatibility report that breaks down how each tool aligns with specific criteria. Users can also generate a detailed PDF implementation guide, making it easy to integrate the AI tool into their current workflow. Building Elytra was an incredible learning experience and I hope to continue building more full-stack applications like it in the future. Huge thanks to the sponsors, organizers, and hackers for making this hackathon possible! ...more ...more

Everyone's worried about moving too slowly with AI. Almost nobody worries about moving too fast until Legal gets involved. A team rolls out a new AI tool, and there’s an instant spike in productivity, which everyone is happy about. A few months later, security discovers customer data has been processed on infrastructure nobody approved. And now, all of a sudden, your success story becomes an audit process. Speed is key. But speed without governance means technical debt that will inevitably need to be repaid down the road. That's why we built gammaNext differently. It runs natively inside Salesforce, keeps the model in your own Azure environment, and logs every action with permission controls. You get the benefits of AI without losing visibility or control over your data. How is your team balancing AI adoption with governance? I'd be interested to hear what's worked and what hasn't.

Hi, my name is Gary, an incoming sophomore at Berkeley with a very normal resume. To stand out, I asked AI to build my personal portfolio. It took 30 seconds. The portfolio was good. That was the problem. Everything AI builds is excellent. Unfortunately, excellence is relativistic. AI-generated personal websites classified as “slop” and “unimpressive” today would’ve been impressive just three years prior. The quality of these websites have not changed, but rather that AI has made their “excellence” common. It is important to realize that AI converges things to the average. Such means that if you purely rely on AI’s spec and taste, the results you produce will likely be “common” and thus, “average” as well. To make myself stand out, I have therefore decided to offer my unreasonably, most delightful personality (source: mother) on a website instead. It’s built in a three dimensional world, and I think it’s worth checking out if you’re not too busy. If you also have a website, put it down below. I would love to check out yours too. Also, for those with questions, I’m happy to share on how I built my website, just ask! To practice what I preach, no AI has been used in the making of this post :).

We won 1st place Grand Prize (and 5K) @ UC Berkeley's AI Hackathon in the Dev Tools Track, out of ~400 teams! We built Ironbook. Photo a machine with your phone. We create a 3D scene. So, we followed passion and built something physical — the first way for LLMs to interact with your nearby 3D world. Y Combinator 's motto is "make something people want." I grew up watching two people do exactly that. 32 years ago, my mom started a business from a tiny basement in India with no funding or family backing. She believed in herself and set a goal to design and stitch clothes that people wanted. My dad was just a friend at the time. He helped out while waiting for his U.S. master's visa. When the opportunity finally came, he made the biggest decision of his life and turned it down because he believed in her. They built the business together. Somewhere along the way, they fell in love and got married. Three decades later, they still run it. Their success came from caring deeply. They remembered the small details, went above and beyond for every customer, and treated employees like family. Some of those customers and employees have been with them for more than 20 years. Over the years, they served more than 100,000 people without spending a dollar on marketing. All word of mouth. Their customers became their community and that community became their growth engine. What I learned from them is simple: - Do the unscalable things to build trust and relationships. - Conviction comes before evidence. - Show up every single day. Through every high and low, I never felt the weight of the business at home. Only now do I understand how deliberate that was. The journey always mattered more to them than the milestones. No matter how ambitious or delusional my ideas sounded, I was never told to play it safe. They believed in me unconditionally. Looking back, it was probably inevitable that I would start something of my own. I grew up curious about the physical world. Scout camps, books, questions like why one crop grows only in a dry season or why the same storm floods one town and not the next. That curiosity is a big part of why we are building Mireye (YC S26) . AI agents are starting to act in the real world, but they can't reliably understand it. Ask a model a specific question about a specific place and it guesses. We’re building the infrastructure to change that. Our mission is to index every inch of the earth and make it as queryable as the web. For three decades, my parents built something people wanted. Now it is our turn.
